content:
A founder I work with had a keynote on Thursday. 24 slides, in front of a room of enterprise buyers.
The deck was strong. The question I kept coming back to: would every claim in it survive someone in the audience checking?

That is the part that usually gets skipped. The usual check is a read-through the night before, and a read-through catches typos, not claims. Slides get reused, numbers carry over from last year's deck, a customer logo goes in because the deal felt close.

So before the rehearsal, I asked the AI employee in my Slack to check every claim against what the company could actually prove.

31 claims across 24 slides.

26 held, each with its source linked in the speaker notes.

3 named customers who had never agreed to be named.

2 numbers came from last year's deck. The July board update had the current ones.

He changed nothing on his own. The founder's name is on the stage, so the founder decides.

When I said go, he swapped in the July numbers and put 3 one-line emails in her drafts, asking those customers for their OK. She sent them herself.

On a stage, trust is built one claim at a time. It is lost the same way.

Would you rather cut a strong claim, or keep one you cannot prove?

comment: The overlooked piece is ownership of evidence. Claim verification works best when sources are maintained continuously, not just before a big event. Trust compounds when every metric has a clear owner.
